stimulus.source_note: Homestead Act, May 20, 1862, Section 1. Public domain.
stimulus.text: That any person who is the head of a family, or who has arrived at the age of twenty-one years, and is a citizen of the United States... shall... be entitled to enter one quarter section or a less quantity of unappropriated public lands...

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from the Homestead Act, May 20, 1862, Section 1, public domain
stem: Under the Homestead Act, how much land could a claimant enter?

options.misconception: 640 acres was the grant for a married couple under the Donation Land Claim Act in Oregon, not the Homestead Act.
The act set a $10 filing fee, not a ten-acre plot.

options.text: As much land as the claimant could fence in a year.
options.misconception: The act fixed the amount at one quarter section; it did not let claimants take whatever they could fence.

rationales.A: A full section of 640 acres was the married couple's grant under Oregon's Donation Land Claim Act of 1850, not the Homestead Act.
rationales.B: The act entitled a claimant to “one quarter section or a less quantity of unappropriated public lands” — 160 acres.
rationales.C: Ten dollars was the filing fee under the act, not the size of the claim.
rationales.D: The act fixed the claim at one quarter section; there was no rule about fencing what one could in a year.
rationales.general:
1. Read the amount in the passage. The act says “one quarter section or a less quantity of unappropriated public lands.”
2. Do the arithmetic. A section is 640 acres, so a quarter section is 160 acres.
3. Keep the other numbers straight. Ten dollars was the fee, and 640 acres belonged to a different law in Oregon.
Remember: numbers in laws are easy to swap. Match each number to its law — 160 acres, Homestead, 1862.
